tagline.text: A natural limestone sinkhole pool connected to the sea, tucked into the coastal village of Anda in Bohol

location.label: Location
location.text: Barangay Bacong, Anda, Bohol (on the road from Anda town toward Talisay Beach)

best_season.label: Best time to visit
best_season.text: Best on clear days (usually drier from March to May)

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱100–1,200 (local transport, entrance and parking in Anda, including a scooter rental from Panglao)

children.text: Cabagnow Cave Pool is a limestone sinkhole hidden in a coconut grove in the village of Anda at the eastern tip of Bohol. Below a round opening a few meters across lies blue water connected to the sea. You climb down a steel ladder or jump in to swim, and it is said to be the largest of Anda's scattered cave pools, which makes it the signature experience of a trip to Anda.

Cabagnow Cave Pool is a natural sinkhole swimming spot in Barangay Bacong, in the village of Anda at the eastern end of Bohol. Locals spell and pronounce the name in a few ways, such as "Kabagno" or "Cabognaw", and OpenStreetMap lists it as a cave entrance (cave_entrance). In Bohol, where limestone is everywhere, the ceiling of a cave collapsed and water filled the hole, so it is often compared to a Mexican cenote. It sits beside the road from Anda town to Talisay Beach, so it is only a little over five minutes by vehicle from the town center.
From above it looks like a small round hole fenced with bamboo stakes, but once you go down you find a deep blue pool surrounded by rock walls. Caving references describe the opening as about
5 m
wide and about
8 m
long, with walls about
5 m
high, water about
deep and a tidal range of about
2 m
. Other travel reports give the deepest point as about 20 feet (about
6 m
). The figures differ from source to source and change with the tide, so treat them as rough.

Because the pool is linked to the sea, the water is not pure fresh water. It is seawater or brackish water (a mix of sea and fresh water), and the level and clarity change with the tide. Visitors report small fish in the pool and stalactites hanging from the ceiling. Larger cave chambers are said to continue beneath the upper wall, but ordinary visitors do not explore them.

Anda is known for several cave pools, including Combento, Cateres, Kaligoon, Tiburako and East Coast. Cabagnow is considered the largest and one of the easiest to reach, so it is usually the first stop for travelers spending a day in Anda. A smaller cave pool, Tibaw, lies farther along the same path and is easy to visit at the same time. Anda sits at the eastern end of the main island of Bohol, and its mood is quite different from the tourist hub of Panglao. Beach resorts and dive shops have multiplied, but it still feels like a quiet fishing town, which suits travelers who want to take their time rather than follow a crowded tour route.

blocks.title: Jumping in and using the ladder

children.text: Depending on the source, the drop from the edge to the water is described as roughly
. You can climb down the steel ladder slowly or jump in. Check that a ladder is in place before you jump.

blocks.title: Blue water linked to the sea

children.text: The pool holds seawater or brackish water, so it is a deep blue-green and its clarity changes with the tide. The round patch of sky and the coconut fronds seen from the water make good photos.

blocks.title: One of Anda's largest cave pools

children.text: It is described as the biggest and most beautiful of Anda's cave pools. With an opening about
5 m
wide and
8 m
long, there is room for several people to swim together.
Stalactites hang from the ceiling and small fish are said to live in the water. Both are often cited as signs that the pool is connected to the sea.
From the parking area to the pool, a dirt path runs between coconut palms with signs along the way. It takes only a few minutes on foot, so it is an easy short visit.
A smaller cave pool, Tibaw, lies about a
5-minute
walk from the same fork in the path. It is about
3 m
deep and is said to have seating and shade around it.
Quinale Beach, a long beach near Anda town, is close by, so a swim in the pool in the morning and a rest at the beach in the afternoon fit together naturally.
One source says there is a lifeguard, that the pool admits 20 people at a time, that stays are limited to about
2 hours
and that life vests can be borrowed. On-site rules can change, so follow the staff.

items.title: Half-day plan
items.subtitle: Enjoying the cave pool and Anda's beaches

children.text: After breakfast at your hotel in Anda town, pack swimwear, shoes you do not mind getting wet, a towel and a waterproof bag.
Ride a scooter or tricycle to the parking area on the road toward Talisay Beach, and pay the entrance and parking fees.
Follow the signed dirt path through the coconut grove to the pool. Check the ladder and the on-site rules (visitor and time limits).
Climb down the ladder, or jump in once you have checked that it is safe. Swim within the visitor and time limits you are given.
Get out and dry off, then go back to the fork and look at Tibaw Cave Pool.
Return to Anda town for lunch, then relax at Quinale Beach in the afternoon.
Water levels change with the tide, so the height of the jump can differ by time of day even on the same day. Follow local guidance first.

items.title: Day trip from Panglao
items.subtitle: Anda's cave pools and a beach

children.text: Leave your Panglao hotel by scooter, or by rental car or van. The distance from Panglao to Anda is about
115 km
, and one report quotes about
2 hours 30 minutes
Arrive in Anda and visit Cabagnow Cave Pool first.
Have lunch at a restaurant in Anda town and take a walk on Quinale Beach.
If you have time, look at nearby beaches such as Talisay Beach.
Set off so that you are back before dark. The one-way trip is long, so avoid driving after sunset.
A day trip involves a lot of travel and can be tiring. If you can, spend a night in Anda.
From Manila, fly to Bohol-Panglao International Airport (TAG), or go to Bohol by way of Cebu. Airlines and schedules change by season, so check when you book.
From the airport to Anda is about
115 km
; by rental car or van, allow about
2 hours 30 minutes–3 hours
The trip from the airport to Anda is long, so decide how you will get there in advance to match your flight arrival time.
Fast ferries (OceanJet, Supercat and others) run several times a day from Cebu City to Tagbilaran Port and are listed as taking about
2 hours
From Tagbilaran, take a bus or van to Anda from Dao Terminal. One report gives about
by bus and about

items.title: By bus or van from Tagbilaran

children.text: One report says that if you take an Anda-bound bus or van and get off in Barangay Bacong, the pool is about a
10-minute
walk from the road.
If no Anda-bound vehicle is available, take one bound for Jagna or Ubay, get off at the Guindulman–Anda junction and hire a tricycle.
From Anda town to the pool is about
5 minutes
by vehicle. A scooter or tricycle is convenient.
Park at the parking area on the road to Talisay Beach and follow the signs on foot.
There is no closed season, and a clear day is best. In general, the drier season means clearer water and calmer seas at Anda's beaches, which makes planning easier.

Right after heavy rain the dirt path to the pool is slippery and the water can turn cloudy. Swimming has been reported as restricted on Mondays and Fridays (check the latest information), so avoid those days and go in the morning to be safe.

and may vary depending on local conditions.

There are no large restaurants around Cabagnow Cave Pool, so it is easiest to eat in Anda town. Anda is a small village, with lodging and restaurants scattered along the town and the coast, and many places in town are within walking distance of Quinale Beach.

Lodging ranges from guesthouses and homestays to beach resorts. Reviews mention places such as Amun Ini Beach Resort, Parklane Bohol Resort and Anda Divers. The prices are old, so check current rates on a booking site.

You can find food at small restaurants in Anda town and at beach resort restaurants. There are almost no shops near the pool, so buy water and snacks in town beforehand and have lunch back in town after your visit. Seafood and Filipino home cooking are the basics, and prices vary by restaurant, so check the menu.

Check first whether a ladder is in place. One report says there was no ladder, so visitors could not enter the water, while another says a ladder was borrowed from a local. If you jump without a ladder, you may have no way out, so never do that.
Before you jump, check the landing area for rocks and floating objects. Limestone is sharp, so non-slip shoes are a good idea.
If you cannot swim, use a life vest or float. Information says life vests can be rented, but confirm on site.
Limits such as 20 people and a stay of about
2 hours
have been reported, so follow the instructions on site.
Bring a towel, a change of clothes, a waterproof bag and a little cash. There are almost no ATMs or shops nearby.
Swimming has been reported as not allowed on Mondays and Fridays. Ask your hotel or a local about opening days before you go.
The path crosses private property, so respect local guidance and signs. Take your trash with you.
Put your camera and phone in waterproof cases, and leave them with someone before you jump.
If you come on a day trip from Panglao, reports say it is about
2 hours 30 minutes
one way to Anda, so start early. Staying a night in Anda lets you enjoy the pool and the beaches without rushing.
The only way out of the pool is the ladder, so do not go in on a day when there is no ladder. It is a seawater pool, so conditions change with the tide.
The presence and condition of the ladder differ from visit to visit. Always check on site.
Jumping carries a high risk of injury. Do not enter the water after drinking, and children must be with an adult.
Entrance fees, hours, closing days and visitor limits differ by source, so follow the latest local guidance.
After rain the dirt path is slippery and the pool water can turn cloudy.
The path is dark after sunset, so leave before dark.
You pass through private property, so follow the signs and local guidance and do not leave the marked route.
The village of
Anda
has Quinale Beach and other beaches as well as other cave pools, so it is easy to combine them with Cabagnow in a one-day itinerary.
A small cave pool about a
5-minute
walk from the fork on the same path, about
3 m
deep.
A long white-sand beach close to Anda town, good for resting after you have played in the pool.
Chocolate Hills
, Bohol's best-known attraction, can be added to a day plan by driving from Anda.
Can-umantad Falls
in northeastern Bohol can be visited in the same trip as Anda.
